milestones.label: 20 minutes
milestones.title: Heart rate starts to settle
milestones.body: Within about 20 minutes your heart rate starts to come down toward its normal resting level.
milestones.note: ACS and NHS sources say heart rate and blood pressure both start to drop; CDC's archived timeline mentions heart rate only.

milestones.label: 12 hours
milestones.title: Carbon monoxide is clearing
milestones.body: Carbon monoxide from smoke is clearing from your blood, so your blood can carry more oxygen.
milestones.note: Sources disagree: older CDC/ACS timelines say about 12 hours to normal; the current CDC page says several days to reach non-smoker levels; some NHS pages say 24-48 hours. 'Clearing' is the cautious claim.

milestones.label: 24 hours
milestones.title: Nicotine is mostly out of your blood
milestones.body: Nicotine drops to very low levels in your blood within about a day, which is why withdrawal begins to bite.
milestones.note: Nicotine's by-products (cotinine) stay detectable for days in tests.

milestones.label: 48 hours
milestones.title: Taste and smell may start to improve
milestones.body: NHS information says that around two days in, taste and smell can start to sharpen as your body adjusts.
milestones.note: Attributed to NHS timelines. We have not included the common claim that nerve endings regrow at 48 hours; we could not confirm it in a primary source.

milestones.label: 3 days
milestones.title: Withdrawal is usually at its worst
milestones.body: Cravings, irritability and poor sleep commonly peak around day 3. This is the hardest stretch, and it does ease.
milestones.note: Individual experience varies; some people peak earlier or later.

milestones.label: ~3 days
milestones.title: Breathing may feel easier
milestones.body: Some people notice breathing feels easier and energy picks up around day 3 as airways relax.
milestones.note: Reported by NHS timelines but evidence is weaker than for long-term outcomes; not everyone notices it this early.

milestones.label: 1 week
milestones.title: Your first full week
milestones.body: The sharpest withdrawal is behind you for most people. Cravings are still frequent but usually shorter.
milestones.note: General pattern from NHS quit-smoking guidance; this is not a precisely measured milestone.

milestones.label: 2 weeks
milestones.title: Withdrawal symptoms are easing
milestones.body: For most people, withdrawal symptoms fade over roughly 2 to 4 weeks. Cravings still come, but less often.
milestones.note: Some people have occasional cravings for months.

milestones.label: 4 weeks
milestones.title: Circulation begins to improve
milestones.body: Over the first weeks to months, blood flow starts to improve, which can make walking and exercise feel easier.
milestones.note: NHS timelines give a range (commonly 2-12 weeks); we picked a conservative point inside it.

milestones.label: 3 months
milestones.title: Coughing and breathlessness start to ease
milestones.body: From about 1-3 months, many people cough less as the lungs' cilia recover and lung function starts to improve.
milestones.note: ACS: coughing and shortness of breath decrease 1-9 months after quitting. Many people cough more for a short time first.

milestones.label: 9 months
milestones.title: Lung function may be up to ~10% better
milestones.body: By about 9 months, lung function may be improved by up to around 10% for some people, with less coughing.
milestones.note: Figure is 'up to'; actual gains depend on how long and how much you smoked.

milestones.label: 1 year
milestones.title: Heart disease risk is about half
milestones.body: After a year, your extra risk of coronary heart disease is roughly half that of someone still smoking.
milestones.note: CDC states heart disease risk falls sharply 1-2 years after quitting; the 'about half' figure is from ACS.

milestones.label: 5 years
milestones.title: Stroke risk keeps falling
milestones.body: Your risk of stroke continues to fall, and can approach that of a non-smoker within about 5 to 10 years.
milestones.note: Sources vary (ACS: as soon as 2-5 years; CDC: 5-10 years). We show the more conservative window.

milestones.label: 5 years
milestones.title: Mouth, throat and bladder cancer risk falls
milestones.body: At around 5 years, risk of cancers of the mouth, throat, oesophagus and bladder is roughly half what it would be if you kept smoking.
milestones.note: Figure applies to people who smoked; cervical cancer risk is also reported to fall to non-smoker levels about 5 years after quitting.

milestones.label: 10 years
milestones.title: Lung cancer death risk is about half
milestones.body: Ten years after quitting, your risk of dying from lung cancer is about half that of someone who kept smoking.
milestones.note: Risk stays higher than that of someone who never smoked.

milestones.label: 15 years
milestones.title: Heart disease risk is near a non-smoker's
milestones.body: Your risk of coronary heart disease is close to that of someone who never smoked.
milestones.note: Older CDC/ACS timelines say 'same as a non-smoker'; we use 'close to' to stay cautious.

milestones.label: 20 years
milestones.title: Long-term risks keep shrinking
milestones.body: Risks of several smoking-related cancers and lung disease continue to decline, and some, such as pancreatic cancer, may approach non-smoker levels.
milestones.note: Some risks (especially lung cancer for heavy long-term smokers) never fully return to never-smoker levels. Specific 20-year claims were not re-verified.

perCigarette.summary: A 2024 UCL analysis in the journal Addiction estimates each cigarette smoked shortens life by about 20 minutes on average (about 17 for men, 22 for women), up from an 11-minute estimate in 2000.
perCigarette.sourceName: Jackson, Jarvis & West, Addiction (Dec 2024), as reported by Dentistry.co.uk
